title: Insecure deserialization
brief: 17:05. The portal stores each customer's preferences in a cookie, so the server does not need a database lookup. The server reads that cookie back into an object.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The cookie is chosen by the customer, and the server rebuilds whatever it says.
teaches: Never rebuild objects from data the user controls: the data decides what code runs
Parse plain data (JSON) and validate every field, or keep the state on the server
Blocking one class name is a blocklist; signing the cookie means the client cannot change it

value.title: Customer preferences cookie

lines: req.prefs = objpack.load(raw);     // rebuilds whatever objects the data names
run() { return execSync(this.cmd); }   // used by the admin tools

value.intro: The cookie is a base64 blob. Decode it, change it, and send it back. Nothing here is a real exploit: it is a made up serialisation format on a made up server.

attempts.response:
HTTP 200
Admin menu shown. The server trusted a field it should never accept from the client.

fix.step: Pick the fix that closes the hole
fix.prompt: Pick every change that stops the cookie choosing what the server builds, and that stops it being changed at all.

options.label: Parse the cookie as plain JSON and validate every field against a schema
code: + req.prefs = validate(PREFS_SCHEMA, JSON.parse(raw));   // only theme, language; nothing else
options.why: Plain data cannot name a class. Anything not in the schema is rejected, including isAdmin.

options.label: Sign the cookie and reject it if the signature does not verify
options.why: The customer can still read it, but cannot change a byte without the server noticing.

options.label: Keep anything that matters on the server, keyed by the session id
options.why: A cookie should hold an id, not the state. Roles and permissions never belong in it.

options.label: Refuse cookies that mention ShellTask
options.why: There are other classes to abuse, and other ways to write the name. A blocklist of class names is never finished.

options.label: Encode the cookie twice so it is harder to read
options.why: Encoding is not integrity. Anyone can decode it, change it and encode it back.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first

card.title: The cookie picked the code
body: The server rebuilt whatever object the cookie named, so a customer changed “Prefs” to “ShellTask” and the server ran a command for them. Another edit added a field the server never should have believed.
Deserialising data the user controls hands them a way to choose your code.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Parsing plain JSON against a schema means the cookie can only ever say a theme and a language. Signing means the customer cannot change it, and holding the important state on the server means there is nothing valuable in the cookie at all.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Data is data, and it cannot be tampered with
body: Parsing plain JSON against a schema means the cookie can only ever say a theme and a language. Signing means the customer cannot change it, and holding the important state on the server means there is nothing valuable in the cookie at all.
Never deserialise untrusted data into objects.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Refusing ShellTask stops that class. The format still lets a cookie choose what to build, so the next dangerous class, or the next spelling, works. Encoding twice protects nothing.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: One name blocked, the rest open
body: Refusing ShellTask stops that class. The format still lets a cookie choose what to build, so the next dangerous class, or the next spelling, works. Encoding twice protects nothing.
Use a format that cannot name code, and make it tamper proof.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
